metric_rationale: This metric isolates trials where Take The Best (TTB) and Tallying make opposite, deterministic predictions. It calculates the proportion of these diagnostic trials where the subject's choice matches the TTB prediction. Under the TTB model, this proportion will be close to 1 (minus response noise). Under the Tallying model, this proportion will be close to 0 (since Tallying always prefers the opposite option). This yields a massive and stable separation between the two theories.

The experimental design includes specific trials where Tallying and Take The Best (TTB) have strictly opposite preferences (e.g., A=[1, 0, 0, 0] vs B=[0, 1, 1, 1]). This metric isolates all trials where Tallying makes a deterministic prediction (i.e., no tie in tally counts) and calculates the proportion of choices that align with Tallying. Data simulated under Tallying will yield high values (approaching 1.0 for low noise), whereas data simulated under TTB will yield very low values (approaching 0.0), perfectly discriminating the two models.

The metric computes the proportion of choices that align with the Weighted Additive (WADD) model on the subset of critical trials where WADD and Tallying make diametrically opposed predictions. Specifically, in trials where one option has 2 highly valid features and the other has 3 less valid features, WADD predicts a preference for the 2-feature option (due to a higher weighted sum), while Tallying predicts a preference for the 3-feature option (due to a higher unweighted count). This metric will yield values close to 1.0 for WADD and close to 0.0 for Tallying, providing a massive and stable contrast.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that are consistent with the Tallying heuristic strictly on the critical dissociation trials (Trials 1 and 2). In these trials, one option has 3 low-validity features (winning the tally 3-to-2) while the other has 2 high-validity features (winning the weighted sum 1.90 to 1.65). Tallying strongly predicts choosing the option with 3 features, whereas WADD strongly predicts choosing the option with 2 high-validity features. The metric will evaluate to a high value (near 1) under Tallying and a low value (near 0) under WADD.

This metric computes the proportion of trials where the subject's choice matches the prediction of the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic. In the experimental design, the trials are specifically constructed such that the most valid discriminating cue points to one option, while a simple tally of all cues favors the opposite option in 4 out of 5 cases (and ties in the 5th). Therefore, simulated TTB agents will have a match rate close to 1.0, whereas simulated Tallying agents will have a match rate close to 0.1 (mostly choosing the opposite, with some guessing on the tie). This produces a massive, robust separation between the two theories.

This metric isolates the critical dissociation trials where the two theories make diametrically opposed predictions. It filters for trials where the option with the highest-validity cue (favored by Take The Best) has strictly fewer total winning cues than the other option (favored by Tallying). By computing the proportion of choices that align with the Take The Best prediction on these specific trials, we achieve a near-perfect contrast: data simulated under Take The Best will yield values close to 1.0, while data simulated under Tallying will yield values close to 0.0. The metric ignores tie trials and baseline agreement trials, ensuring maximum sensitivity and low within-theory variance.

Under the Tallying heuristic, Trial 1 and Trial 2 both feature Option A winning on exactly 1 fewer feature than Option B (A wins 2 vs 3 in Trial 1; A wins 1 vs 2 in Trial 2). Thus, Tallying predicts an identical choice probability for Option A across both trials, leading to an expected difference of 0. Under the WADD model, the weighted sum of validities produces different relative preference strengths for these two trials, meaning the difference in choice probability for Option A should systematically deviate from 0.

To reliably discriminate the theories regardless of the adversary's parameter distribution (particularly the sign of WADD's gamma), we measure the *determinism* of choices on 'tie' trials. Trials 2, 6, and 8 feature options that each win on exactly two features. Because Tallying completely ignores validities, it evaluates these pairs as perfect ties and guesses uniformly at random (50% probability), yielding an absolute deviation from 0.5 near zero (bounded only by binomial sampling noise). In contrast, WADD uses the validities to break these ties. Even if WADD's gamma parameter varies widely across subjects (causing some to consistently prefer A and others to consistently prefer B depending on whether gamma is positive or negative), any individual WADD subject will exhibit a strong, deterministic preference on each of these trial types. By calculating the absolute deviation from 0.5 per trial type *within* each subject and averaging, we obtain a metric that is robustly low for Tallying and robustly high for WADD, with minimal between-subject variance.

This metric isolates 'tie' trials where both options win on an equal number of features. Under pure Tallying, the decision-maker has no basis for preference on these trials and must guess, resulting in an expected choice probability of exactly 0.5. However, under the advocated mixture model, the Take-The-Best (TTB) component will deterministically break the tie using the highest-validity discriminating cue. By measuring the proportion of choices that align with the TTB prediction on these specific tied trials, we can cleanly dissociate the two theories: pure Tallying will yield ~0.5, whereas the mixture model will yield a value significantly greater than 0.5, proportional to the mixture weight of the TTB strategy.

This metric isolates the proportion of decisions that align with the Take-The-Best (TTB) heuristic specifically on trials where the Tallying heuristic predicts a 50/50 tie (i.e., both options have an equal number of winning features). Under the Tallying model, this proportion will be exactly 0.5 (subject to binomial noise). Under the Mixture model, the TTB component breaks these ties deterministically according to the highest-validity cue, pushing the proportion significantly above 0.5.

Trial 5 presents a case where Option A has the two highest validity features, while Option B has the next two features. Under Tallying, this is a 2-to-2 tie, so subjects guess uniformly (50% choice of A). Under the advocated Thresholded WADD model, the weighted value difference is large (0.311). Since the threshold parameter is drawn from [0.0, 0.5], over 60% of simulated subjects will have a threshold below 0.311, meaning they will rely on WADD and choose Option A reliably. Measuring the proportion of Option A choices on this specific trial yields a sharp divergence between the two models' predictions.

In Trial 3, Option A wins on 2 features and Option B wins on 2 features. The advocated Tallying model sees this as a perfect tie and predicts exactly a 50% chance of choosing Option A, regardless of its beta or epsilon parameters. The between-subject variance under Tallying will strictly be the binomial sampling variance. However, the competing Thresholded WADD model evaluates the weighted additive difference. Because Option A wins on the two highest-validity features, its WADD score is substantially higher than Option B's (a difference of ~0.225). For the ~45% of subjects whose threshold is drawn below this difference, the competing model will use the WADD strategy and deterministically favor Option A, driving P(A) near 1.0. For the rest, it falls back to Tallying (0.5). By isolating Trial 3 rather than averaging it with other tie trials (which have negligible WADD differences and dilute the signal), we maximize the mean difference between the two theories while keeping the Tallying variance at the theoretical minimum.

Under the Competing Theory (Tallying), trials 2 and 8 result in exact ties (2 feature wins for A, 2 for B), so the probability of choosing either option is 0.5. The metric sums the proportion of choosing A in trial 2 and B in trial 8, which yields an expected value of 1.0 under Tallying. Under the Advocated Theory, both Left-to-Right Take-The-Best and the Top-Heavy Penalty strongly agree on A in trial 2 and on B in trial 8. Because these trials are 'Tally Ties', the Advocated Theory boosts the weight of the Top-Heavy Penalty, leading to a much higher expected value (> 1.0) for this metric.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Top-Heavy Penalty (THP) strategy specifically on trials where the Pure Tallying heuristic results in a tie. Under the Advocated Theory (Pure Tallying), subjects guess randomly on these trials, producing a mean alignment of 0.5. Under the Competing Theory, the THP weight is significantly boosted during tally ties to act as a decisive tie-breaker. Because the distribution of w_thp_tie [0, 50] is much larger than w_ltr [0, 10], the THP strategy will dominate the choice on these tie trials, resulting in an alignment proportion substantially higher than 0.5.

This metric isolates trials where the primary Tallying heuristic results in a tie (i.e., both options have the same number of strict feature-wise wins). According to Pure Tallying, subjects will guess randomly on these trials, yielding a match rate of exactly 0.5 to any arbitrary tie-breaking rule. The Advocated Theory, however, posits that subjects use a recency/anti-primacy tie-breaker, favoring the option whose positive features appear later in the sequence. By computing the proportion of tie trials where the subject chooses the option favored by the recency weights, we expect a value significantly higher than 0.5 for the Advocated Theory, cleanly discriminating it from Pure Tallying.

The metric computes the proportion of choices that align with the recency tie-breaker on trials where the primary Tallying heuristic results in a tie. Under the Advocated Theory (Pure Tallying), subjects will guess uniformly at random on these trials, yielding a metric value around 0.5. Under the Competing Theory (Tallying with Recency), subjects systematically break ties using the recency score, yielding a metric value strictly greater than 0.5.

This metric isolates 'Tallying Tie' trials, where both options have an equal number of positive features. The Competing Theory (Pure Tallying) has no basis for preference on these trials and predicts uniform 50/50 guessing, leading to choice proportions near 0.5 (with only binomial noise). The Advocated Theory, however, resolves these ties either by sticking with the Take-The-Best winner (if the threshold is not met) or by using the Recency tie-breaker. Both mechanisms produce deterministic preferences (modulo response noise). By calculating the absolute deviation of the choice proportion from 0.5 for each tie trial type and averaging, we obtain a metric that is near zero for Pure Tallying but significantly positive for the Advocated Theory.

This metric calculates the mean absolute deviation of the choice probability from 0.5 on 'Tally Tie' trials (where both options have an equal number of feature wins). The Advocated Theory (Pure Tallying) predicts exactly 50/50 guessing on these trials, so the sample proportion will be close to 0.5 (yielding a small absolute deviation governed only by binomial variance). The Competing Theory, however, will resolve these ties deterministically either via Take-The-Best (if the opposing wins are below threshold) or via the recency tie-breaker. This results in choice probabilities near 0 or 1, yielding a mean absolute deviation close to 0.5.

On 'Tie' trials where both options have the same number of positive features (and the same number of feature-wise wins), the pure Tallying model is completely indifferent and guesses uniformly at random (50/50). Consequently, a subject's proportion of choosing option A on these specific trial pairs will center around 0.5, with deviations driven purely by binomial noise. The Soft WADD model, however, integrates the explicit validities and a spatial position bias. Because the position bias varies wildly between subjects (w_pos in [-5, 5]), Soft WADD will usually have a strong, deterministic preference for one option over the other on these tie trials. By measuring the mean absolute deviation from 0.5 for each unique tie pair within each subject, we can distinctly separate Tallying (small deviation, ~0.14 for 16 reps) from Soft WADD (large deviation, approaching 0.5 minus lapse rate).

This metric isolates the 'Tally Tie' trials, where both options have an equal number of strict feature-wise wins. Under the pure Tallying theory, decision-makers have no basis for preference on these trials and must guess, meaning the true choice probability is exactly 0.5. The metric calculates the mean choice probability for each of these trial types per subject, and measures the absolute deviation from 0.5. For Tallying, this deviation will merely reflect binomial sampling noise (which is small and predictable). For the Competing Theory (Soft WADD), validities and position biases will systematically push preferences away from 0.5, resulting in a much larger absolute deviation.

This metric calculates the proportion of times a subject chooses the option with the higher validity score specifically on trials where the tally counts are tied. The Competing Theory (Pure Tallying) predicts a 50/50 guess on these tie trials, yielding a metric value near 0.5. The Advocated Theory (Tallying with Strict Validity Tie-Breaking) predicts a systematic preference for the option with higher validity, yielding a metric value significantly greater than 0.5.

To perfectly isolate the Competing Theory's validity tie-breaker, this metric calculates the proportion of choices favoring the higher-validity option strictly on 'Tally Tie' trials. Under Pure Tallying, this proportion is exactly 0.5 in expectation. To drastically reduce the binomial noise variance from random guessers (low beta or high epsilon) without introducing bias, the deviation from 0.5 is multiplied by a continuous weight derived from the subject's accuracy on 'Strict Win' trials. Because strict win accuracy and tie-trial choices are independent under the Advocated Theory, the expected value remains exactly 0.0 with extremely tight variance. Under the Competing Theory, highly deterministic subjects exhibit both high strict accuracy and strong validity tie-breaking, ensuring a robustly positive signal.

The metric isolates 'Tally Tie' trials where both options have an equal number of strict feature-wise wins. According to the Competing Theory, subjects will guess randomly in these trials, resulting in a 50% chance of choosing either option. According to the Advocated Theory, subjects use an inverse-validity tie-breaker, heavily weighting the lowest validity feature (the 4th feature, index 3). This metric computes the proportion of tie trials where the subject chose the option that possessed the lowest validity feature. The Competing Theory predicts ~0.5, while the Advocated Theory predicts a value significantly >0.5.

This metric isolates the 'Tally Tie' trials, where both options have an equal number of strict feature-wise wins. Under the Advocated Theory (Pure Tallying), subjects should guess randomly on these trials, resulting in an alignment score of 0.5. Under the Competing Theory, subjects use an inverse validity tie-breaker, weighting lower-validity features more heavily. By computing the proportion of tie-trial choices that align with this inverse validity bias, we can cleanly separate the two theories: the Advocated Theory predicts ~0.5, while the Competing Theory predicts a value significantly >0.5.

The metric calculates the proportion of times subjects choose Option B on 'Tally Tie' trials (trials where both options have an equal number of positive features). On these specific trials, the Competing Theory relies on Take-The-Best (TTB) to break the tie, which consistently favors Option A because it has the single highest-validity cue. Conversely, the Advocated Theory uses an inverse validity tie-breaker that strongly weights the lower-validity cues, consistently favoring Option B. Therefore, the Advocated Theory predicts a metric value significantly above 0.5, while the Competing Theory predicts a value significantly below 0.5.

Focuses exclusively on 'Tally Tie' trials, where the two theories make diametrically opposed predictions. The Advocated Theory's Take-The-Best mechanism breaks ties using the highest-validity cue (which always favors option A in these specific ties), leading to a low proportion of B choices. In contrast, the Competing Theory's inverse validity tie-breaker heavily weights the lowest-validity cues (which favor option B), leading to a high proportion of B choices. Measuring the rate of B choices on these tie trials will thus yield a massive, stable gap between the two theories.

Calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Advocated Theory's predictions on the three critical 'Tally Tie' trials. On these trials, the Inverse Validity tie-breaker (Advocated) and the Attention Decay tie-breaker (Competing) make diametrically opposed predictions because the lowest-validity features are positioned on the left, while recency heavily weights the right-most features. A value close to 1.0 supports the Advocated Theory, while a value close to 0.0 supports the Competing Theory.

The two theories diverge heavily on 'Tally Tie' trials. Because of the experimental design, the tie trials consistently pit the right-most features (favored by the Advocated Theory's Attention Decay/Recency mechanism) against the left-most features (favored by the Competing Theory's Inverse Validity mechanism, since they have the lowest validity). Option A always wins on the right-most features, while Option B always wins on the left-most features. Thus, computing the proportion of Option B choices (response == 1) on Tally Tie trials will yield a value close to 0 for the Advocated Theory and close to 1 for the Competing Theory.
